pr.title: Sign in to a hosted Projector service, and post CI reviews as its app with no private key
pr.head: 07251b5e0532c0de9a7f02b4644e9cab47a86605

summary: Projector can review pull requests in GitHub Actions and post each review under a GitHub App's name. Until now that meant registering your own app and storing its private key as a repository secret. This pull request adds the client side of a hosted Projector service: a server that holds the private key of its own app, Projector Review, and hands each CI job a short-lived token for the one repository the job runs in, once someone pays for the installation.

1. The project hosted commands, which sign you in to the service through GitHub, keep the account token in the OS keychain, register your agent.key by answering a sealed challenge, and show, subscribe, claim, and sign out the account.
  2. An app: projector input on the review action, which trades the job's GitHub Actions OIDC token for the service's installation token, so the workflow stores no private key. project init --ci-review --ci-app projector writes that workflow.
The server is not in this pull request; the tests run every command against a fake service on a local port.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Hosted service: the server at hosted.url, by default https://api.projector.bot.
  • Account token: what the service returns after sign-in, kept in the keychain under the service name projector-hosted, keyed by the service's address.
  • OIDC token: a signed token GitHub Actions gives a job with id-token: write, naming the repository and ref, for an audience the job chooses.
  • Destination: a setting that says where your data goes; a value a repository commits applies only after project config allow.
  • agent.key: the X25519 key the relay uses to seal messages and state end to end.

cards.title: What the review found
cards.html:
• Both earlier findings are fixed, and this head is clean.
  • register_key opens only a labelled challenge of exactly 32 random bytes and sends back only those bytes, so a relay record passed off as a challenge is refused.
  • sign_in keeps only a token in the service's form, pjh_ and 43 characters of base64url, and MacOS.store refuses any value that could end its security -i command and start another.
  • The gate and the check job passed.

groups.title: The hosted service client
groups.kicker: The new hosted module and the project hosted commands that drive it
intro: hosted.py is the whole client. Every request goes through one helper, call, which uses urllib alone, so the CLI still has no dependencies. When the service refuses a request, the error carries the service's own words, and a 401 or 402 adds the command or address that fixes it.

Sign-in is GitHub's device flow, run through the service: the CLI prints a code, polls until you approve it, stores the token, and then registers agent.key. To prove it holds the private key, it opens a challenge the service sealed to the key. The challenge is the label projector hosted key challenge v1, a NUL byte, and 32 random bytes, and the CLI sends back only the random bytes. The same key opens your relay records, so the CLI refuses anything else the service seals to it and sends nothing back.
The same module holds review_token_step, the action step for app: projector, described in the CI group.

files.note: New module: the HTTP helper, sign-in, key registration, account, claim, subscribe, logout, and the action's token step.

checks.text: sign_in keeps the token only when it fully matches ACCOUNT_TOKEN, so the keychain never sees a value the service chose outside that form. Checked by reading the new test, which refuses a token with a newline, a quote, or the wrong length, with nothing stored.

register_key refuses a plaintext that is not CHALLENGE_PREFIX followed by exactly CHALLENGE_BYTES bytes, before it sends any answer. Checked by reading the new tests: they refuse a relay-shaped record sealed from agent.key itself and a labelled record of the wrong length, each with one POST /v1/keys and nothing registered.

In CI, address raises NotAllowed, a ConfigError, for a hosted.url the repository commits, so a pull request cannot point the OIDC token at another server; the step fails instead. Checked by reading Config.setting.
Only a pull_request job's refs/pull/<n>/merge ref yields a pull request number; a manual run sends only the repository.

files.note: Adds the hosted subcommands and run_hosted, and teaches ci_app and init_ci_review the projector app, which needs no ID or key secret.

groups.title: A service name for keychain items
groups.kicker: The keychain stores the account token apart from the relay's keys
intro: Before this change the keychain module stored only the relay's private keys, under one fixed service name. Each backend now takes a service argument, which defaults to the relay's, so the account token lives under projector-hosted and every existing caller is unchanged.

files.note: Threads a keyword-only service through the macOS, Linux, and Windows backends and the module's store, read, and delete.

checks.text: MacOS.store refuses a service name, account, or secret holding whitespace, a quote, a backslash, or a control character before anything reaches security -i, which reads its commands from that script. A relay key's base64, its hex key ID, and a hosted.url account contain none of them, so the relay's path is unchanged. Checked by reading UNSCRIPTABLE and the new test, which also stores a real relay key.

groups.title: The hosted.url setting
groups.kicker: A new destination setting that names the service
intro: hosted.url says which service the commands and the action talk to. It is a destination, because the account token goes there, so a value a repository commits applies only once you allow it. hosted_url accepts an https:// address with no path, query, or user info, or http:// on this machine, and normalizes it, because the normalized form is both the keychain account and the OIDC audience.

files.note: Registers hosted.url, adds it to DESTINATIONS, and adds the hosted_url validator.

groups.title: Posting CI reviews as the hosted app
groups.kicker: The action's app input and the workflow init writes for it
intro: With app: projector, the review action runs a new step that asks GitHub Actions for the job's OIDC token, with the service's address as the audience, and posts it to /v1/review-token. The service answers an installation token and its login. The step masks the token, and the review and summary steps use it in place of an app's own token.

init --ci-app projector writes app: projector instead of the key inputs, gives both jobs id-token: write, and adds projector-review[bot] to review.reviewers. A workflow for any other app renders byte for byte as before.

files.note: Adds the app input and the token step, and falls back to its outputs for GH_TOKEN and the login.

checks.text: The context-repository steps still run only with app-id, so a review through the hosted app reads no context repositories, as the docs say.

files.note: Adds HOSTED_APP and HOSTED_LOGIN, and renders the app input and id-token: write for the hosted app.
Adds an @ID_TOKEN@ placeholder after each job's permissions, which renders empty for other apps.

groups.title: Agent permissions
groups.kicker: Agents ask before running project hosted
intro: project hosted holds a credential and can start a subscription, so Claude Code asks before it and the Codex rules leave it to Codex's approval.

files.note: Adds Bash(project hosted *) to the ask rules and names the command in the Codex rules' comment.

groups.title: Tests
groups.kicker: A fake service, the action step in bash, and the workflow init writes
intro: test_hosted.py runs each command against a fake service on a local port that seals real challenges, and runs the action step's script in bash against a fake OIDC endpoint. test_ci.py checks the workflow init --ci-app projector writes.

groups.title: Documentation
groups.kicker: How to sign in and how to post CI reviews through the service
